questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question:
A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation with a prosthetic valve replacement for mitral stenosis is on warfarin therapy. Her INR is 3. What is the appropriate next step in management?

LMWH- Low molecular weight heparin
options: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and asprin
questions.explanation:
The next appropriate step in the management of a pregnant woman with a prosthetic valve on warfarin therapy at 36 weeks of gestation is to stop warfarin and start low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). 

Warfarin is safe and effective in preventing thromboembolism in the mother during the 2nd trimester. However, it is teratogenic and can lead to miscarriage, stillbirths, fetal anticoagulation, and fetal embryopathy if used in the 1st trimester.

Heparin is safe for the fetus as it does not cross the placenta but is less effective than warfarin in preventing thromboembolism.

Period of gestation Anticoagulant

Till 12 completed weeks

 LMWH or UFH
13 to 36 weeks Warfarin
36 weeks till just before delivery LMWH or UFH
6 hours after vaginal delivery and 24 hours after cesarean section Warfarin, LMWH or UFH 

LMWH- Low molecular weight heparin, UFH- Unfractionated heparin 

For patients taking LMWH, factor Xa levels should be monitored weekly.

Heparin should be discontinued just before (at least 6 hours before) delivery. If delivery occurs before discontinuation and there is extensive bleed­ing, then iv protamine sulfate can be given. Warfarin or heparin anticoagulation can be restarted after 6 hours of vaginal delivery, usually without any problem.

Warfarin, LMWH, and UFH do not accumulate in breast milk and do not have an anticoagulant effect in the newborn. They are compatible with breastfeeding.

Other options:

Option B: Unfractionated heparin can also be given instead of LMWH. However, in this case, the better answer is to give LMWH; because, in clinical practice, LMWHs have a long half-life, once-daily dosing, and fewer side effects. If LMWH is unavailable or cost-prohibitive, or if anti-Xa levels cannot be monitored, continuous infusion of UFH can be used as an alternative to LMWH.

Option D: Aspirin 75-100 mg can be given daily during pregnancy. It can be continued in women with mechanical heart valves if needed for other indications.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A 27-year-old female patient was found to have uterus didelphys. Which of the following is not likely to be a complication of this uterine anomaly?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, transverse lie is not a likely complication of uterus didelphys. A transverse lie is more likely to be seen with an arcuate or sub-septate uterus.

A uterus didelphys is a Mullerian defect characterized by two separate uterine horns, each with an endometrial cavity and uterine cervix. It occurs due to the failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts.

It is usually asymptomatic but can rarely present with dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, hematocolpos, and hematometra. Rarely, endometriosis (option B) and genital neoplasms may be associated with uterus didelphys.

Pregnancy is possible with uterus didelphys, however, there is an increased risk of the following complications:

  • Spontaneous abortion (option A)
  • Preterm labor (option C)
  • Breech presentation
  • Cesarean delivery
  • Intrauterine growth restriction
  • Low birth weight (<2.5kg)
  • Perinatal death

Uterus didelphys can be diagnosed with ultrasound or hysterosalpingography, but MRI provides the most accurate diagnosis.

questions.question: A woman who underwent dilatation and curettage for molar pregnancy 6 months ago presents with persistent symptoms of abdominal pain and distention. On further evaluation, the beta-hCG levels were persistently elevated and cannonball foci were found on the chest X-ray. What is the appropriate management in this case?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a woman with a past history of D(&)C for molar pregnancy, now presenting with abdominal pain and distension, elevated beta-HCG levels, and cannonball metastasis to the lung is suggestive of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN).

The next step is to categorize the patient as low/high risk based on the WHO prognostic scoring system to decide the treatment modality. 

WHO Prognostic Scoring System, adapted by FIGO:

 Prognostic Factor Score
0 1 2 4
Age < 40  >40 - -
Antecedent gestation Mole Abortion Term -
Interval in months <4 4-6 7-12 >12
Pretreatment serum hCG (IU/L) < 103 103 to < 104 104 to < 105 > 105
Largest tumor size (including the uterus) <3 3-4 ≥ 5  -
Site of metastases Lung Spleen, kidney GI tract Brain, liver
Number of metastases - 1-4 5-8 >8
Previously failed chemotherapy  - - single drug ≥ 2 drugs
  • Low-risk GTN: score ≤6
  • High-risk GTN: score ≥7

Based on the available clinical information,

  • Antecedent gestation: molar pregnancy, score= 0
  • Interval: 6 months, score= 1
  • Site of metastasis: lung, score= 0

The total score is 1, hence it is a case of low-risk GTN and the management involves treatment with methotrexate with folinic acid.

Treatment of GTN:

Low-risk GTN (FIGO Stages I-III: score <7): Single-agent chemotherapy with methotrexate (MTX) or dactinomycin (less commonly used). 

  • 50 mg MTX is given IM on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 with folinic acid on alternate days.

High-risk GTN (FIGO Stages II-III: score >7 and Stage IV): Multiple agent chemotherapies, with or without adjuvant surgery or radiotherapy. The preferred multiple-agent chemotherapy regime is the EMACO regime:

  • Etoposide
  • Methotrexate
  • Dactinomycin (actinomycin D)
  • Cyclophosphamide
  • Vincristine (Oncovin)

GTN typically develops along with or after a molar pregnancy. Rarely, it may develop after live birth, miscarriage, or medical termination of pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A female patient has a history of three miscarriages. Identify the investigation that was done from the image shown below.
questions.explanation:
The investigation shown in the given image is hysterosalpingography. The given hysterosalpingogram shows a unicornuate uterus.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is an imaging modality in which radiopaque contrast is injected through the cervical canal to assess the endometrial cavity, the fallopian tubes, and the endocervical canal.

HSG should be done between days 5 and 10 of the menstrual cycle, in the preovulatory phase, as an outpatient procedure. Leech Wilkinson cannula, Rubin's cannula, or Foley's catheter no.14 is introduced into the endometrial cavity through the cervical os, and the contrast is injected. The uterine cavity and fallopian tubes are then visualized and X-rays are obtained.

HSG can be used for the following:

  • To assess tubal patency in infertility 
  • To detect uterine anomalies, synechiae, and polyps
  • To detect incompetence of the cervical os

Contraindications to HSG:

  • Acute pelvic infection 
  • Active uterine bleeding
  • Pregnancy/ suspected pregnancy
  • Contrast allergy
  • Premenstrual phase

HSG is a safe procedure, however, complications such as ascending spread of infection, chemical peritonitis, allergic reaction to the dye, or pelvic endometriosis may occur. 



Other options:

Option A: Hysteroscopy is an operative procedure in which the uterine cavity can be visualized by passing a fiberoptic telescope via the cervix. It can be diagnostic or therapeutic. A hysteroscopic image of a uterus with carcinoma is shown below.



Option B: Saline infusion sonography is a procedure where normal saline is injected into the uterine cavity and the uterus is imaged with transvaginal sonography. It is shown in the image below.



Option D: Transvaginal ultrasonography is a noninvasive imaging technique using the transvaginal approach. It provides a more detailed evaluation of the pelvic organs as compared to the transabdominal approach.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A 56-year-old multipara woman presented with grade II/III uterine prolapse with cystocele. She complains of passing urine on coughing and sneezing. What is the type of urinary incontinence seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The type of urinary incontinence present in a patient with prolapse and cystocele experiencing urination on coughing and sneezing is stress incontinence.

Stress incontinence refers to the involuntary leakage of urine when there is increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, coughing, sneezing, laughing, Valsalva maneuver). Absence of detrusor muscle contraction is seen in urodynamic studies.

Causes:

  • Age and menopause - due to estrogen deficiency
  • Multiparity - due to loss of pelvic muscle tone
  • Obesity
  • Smoking
  • Constipation, chronic cough
  • Pelvic organ prolapse
  • Pregnancy - due to the effect of progesterone and pressure of the gravid uterus on the bladder neck.
  • Puerperium - due to descent of the bladder neck, loss of urethro-vesical angle, and reduced pelvic muscle tone 
  • Surgical repair of vesicovaginal fistula

Grading of genuine stress incontinence (GSI) :

  • Grade I: Incontinence with only severe stress, such as coughing, sneezing, and jogging.
  • Grade II: Incontinence with moderate stress, such as fast walk, going up and down the stairs.
  • Grade III: Incontinence with mild stress such as standing.

Investigations are only done prior to surgery to confirm the diagnosis. They include:

  • Stress test
  • Cotton swab or Q-tip test
  • Marshall and Bonney’s test
  • Urethroscopy
  • Urodynamic studies.

These are not required prior to conservative management.

Conservative management includes Kegel's pelvic exercises, electric nerve stimulation, devices like pessaries, vaginal cones, and artificial sphincters. Medical treatment with estrogen creams, alpha agonists, venlafaxine, and imipramine may be useful.

Other options:

Option A: Overflow incontinence is an old term that refers to the inability to empty the bladder, with involuntary, continuous urinary dribbling. Currently, it refers to another presentation of urge incontinence. 

Option B: Urge incontinence is the involuntary escape of urine when there is an imminent need to urinate. It occurs due to detrusor muscle overactivity or detrusor instability. It is seen more commonly in old women with decreased bladder capacity, decreased sensation, and CNS inhibition. 

Option D: Neurogenic bladder occurs in patients with neurogenic dysfunction leading to detrusor hyperreflexia. Conditions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and spinal injury give rise to this. They present with urgency or urge incontinence.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A 32-year-old married woman who came for the evaluation of infertility was found to have a septum in her uterine cavity. What would be the appropriate management of this case?
questions.explanation:
The appropriate management for a 32-year-old woman with a septate uterus is hysteroscopy and septoplasty.

Hysteroscopic septoplasty refers to the resection of the uterine septum under hysteroscopic guidance. The septum can be resected either with a resectoscope or a laser. It does not scar the uterus and avoids the necessity of cesarean sections for future pregnancies. There is a reduced risk of pelvic adhesions, compared with transabdominal approaches.

A septate uterus is characterized by a septum in the endometrial cavity. It is caused by the failure of the medial segments of the Müllerian ducts to regress. This creates a permanent septum within the uterine cavity. 

The septum can project partially from the fundus or extend completely to the cervical os. It is the most common congenital uterine malformation in women with infertility.

Other options:

Option A: Hysterectomy is not advisable since the patient has come for infertility evaluation and desires pregnancy.

Options B & D: Laparoscopy/laparotomy and metroplasty are not preferred for the treatment of a septate uterus due to the following:

  • Requirement of cesarean section for subsequent pregnancies to prevent uterine rupture.
  • Postoperative pelvic adhesions leading to infertility.
Note: Jone's and Tompkin's metroplasties are surgeries for the septate uterus that involve a transabdominal approach. They cause uterine scarring and are hence not preferred.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A 30-year-old G4A3 woman had a history of miscarriage at 8 weeks, the second miscarriage at 11 weeks with no cardiac activity, and the third pregnancy loss at 24 weeks with preterm delivery due to early-onset preeclampsia. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a G4A3 woman with miscarriages at 8 and 11 weeks, and preterm delivery due to preeclampsia at 24 weeks is suggestive of antiphospholipid antibody (APLA) syndrome. 

APLA is an autoimmune disorder commonly associated with fetal death, preterm delivery, early-onset preeclampsia, and fetal growth restriction due to placental insufficiency and thromboses. Pregnancy loss usually occurs before 10 weeks.

Diagnosis of APLA requires at least 1 clinical criterion and 1 laboratory criterion.

  • Obstetric criteria
    • One or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond 10 weeks or
    • Severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency requiring delivery before 34 weeks, or
    • Three or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before 10 weeks
  • Laboratory criteria
    • Presence of lupus anticoagulant, or
    • Anticardiolipin antibodies, or
    • Anti-β2 glycoprotein antibody

Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), also referred to as a recurrent miscarriage or habitual abortion, is historically defined as 3 consecutive pregnancy losses prior to 20 weeks from the last menstrual period. 

Common causes include:

  • Parental chromosomal abnormalities
  • Untreated hypothyroidism
  • Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
  • Uterine anatomic abnormalities,
  • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome 

Other options:

Option A: There is no history of STD or skin lesions suggestive of syphilis and according to Kassawitz rule, in women with untreated syphilis having a series of pregnancies, the likelihood of fetal infection in later pregnancies becomes less; usually, only the first pregnancy is an abortion, the following pregnancy losses will be stillbirths in the next trimester rather than recurrent pregnancy loss.

Option C: TORCH infections may play a role in sporadic spontaneous pregnancy loss, rather than recurrent pregnancy losses.

Option D: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) refers to the onset or first recognition of diabetes during pregnancy, usually at the 24-28 weeks screening test. Women with uncontrolled overt or pregestational diabetes with elevated HbA1c or prepran­dial glucose in the first trimester have an increased risk for early miscarriage, but there is a history or lab findings suggestive of gestational diabetes mellitus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A 26-year-old female patient came with a history of fatiguability and constipation for the past 1 year. She has a history of multiple blood transfusions after delivery 4 years ago. She has had a lactational failure and never regained her periods after the delivery. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in a woman with lactational failure and postpartum amenorrhea, now presenting with fatiguability and constipation is Sheehan syndrome. A history of multiple blood transfusions after delivery indicates major obstetric blood loss, which resulted in pituitary ischemia leading to this condition.

Sheehan syndrome is panhypopituitarism due to pituitary ischemia and necrosis following massive obstetrical hemorrhage.

The most severe form presents with shock due to pituitary apoplexy. It is characterized by a sudden onset headache, nausea, visual deficits, and hormonal dysfunction due to acute pituitary hemorrhage or infarction. Less severe forms present with anovulation and amenorrhea.

Damage to specific pituitary cell types leads to lactational failure, loss of axillary and pubic hair, and symptoms of hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency. Prolactin deficiency is most commonly encountered, but adrenal insufficiency is the most life-threatening complication. Hence, the adrenal function should be immediately assessed if there is any suspicion of Sheehan syndrome.

Option B: Hypothyroidism can present with vague symptoms such as fatigue, constipation, and amenorrhea. However, postpartum hypothyroidism usually presents 4-8 months after delivery after a thyrotoxic phase with palpitations and thyroid enlargement.

Option C: Premature ovarian failure presents with menopausal symptoms. It is due to primary ovarian dysfunction. It is diagnosed when serum FSH levels are >30-40 mIU/mL on two occasions, at least one month apart.

Option D: Delayed transfusion reaction presents days to weeks after the transfusion. It may be asymptomatic or with low-grade fever. Coombs test may be positive, unconjugated bilirubin increased, and the rise in hemoglobin levels following the transfusion will be less than expected.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: The ultrasound of a young woman with infertility is suggestive of a uterine anomaly. Which of the following is used to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, hysteroscopy with laparoscopy is used to confirm the diagnosis. 

For infertility evaluation, hysteroscopy and laparoscopy can detect müllerian anomalies, screen for co-existent endometriosis, and exclude other tubal or uterine cavity pathology.

This approach can differentiate between a septate and a bicornuate uterus. On laparoscopy, the presence of a uterine fundus indicates that the uterus is septate, while its absence indicates it is bicornuate. The capacity of each horn in a bicornuate uterus and the depth and thickness of the uterine septum prior to surgical resection can also be assessed. 

MRI is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of Mullerian anomalies. It clearly delineates both the internal and external uterine anatomy. Complex anomalies and common associations like renal or skeletal anomalies can also be evaluated. It is also less invasive than hysteroscopy and laparoscopy in diagnosing Mullerian anomalies.

Other options:

Option A: Hysterosalpingography (HSG) provides information about the interior contour of the uterine cavity but cannot accurately visualize the external contour of the uterus. 

Option C: Laparoscopy alone as a diagnostic procedure cannot visualize the interior contour of a hollow viscus like the uterus. This can be done only with the help of hysteroscopy or imaging such as sonography, HSG, or MRI.

Option D: Transvaginal sonography is used for the initial detection of uterine anomalies causing infertility or spontaneous abortions. Complete evaluation of these anomalies is done by MRI.

Note: 

  • Hysteroscopy is the gold standard investigation to visualize the uterine cavity and tubal ostia. It also has therapeutic benefits in cases of endometrial polyps, submucous resection of myoma, hysteroscopic adhesiolysis, and resection of uterine septum. 
  • Laparoscopy is the gold standard investigation to evaluate tubal factors of infertility.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A 26-year-old pregnant woman, on examination was found to have infra-umbilical flattening. The fetal heart sounds were heard over the lateral side. What could be the fetal presentation/position?
questions.explanation:
The presence of infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds on the lateral side indicates that the fetus is in the occipito-posterior position.

Occipito-posterior (OP) position of the fetus is when the occiput is situated posteriorly over the sacroiliac joint, or directly over the sacrum. The fetus is in vertex presentation.

Examination findings of OP position:

  • On inspection, the abdomen appears flattened below the umbilicus (infra-umbilical flattening).
  • Pelvic grips:
    • The head is not engaged.
    • The sinciput (cephalic prominence) is not prominently felt.
  • Auscultation: Fetal heart sounds are heard maximally over the flanks. However, in the direct OP position, they are heard in the midline.

There are three variants of OP position:

  • Left OP position (fourth position of the vertex) - When the occiput points towards the left sacroiliac joint. 
  • Right OP position (third position of the vertex) - When the occiput points towards the right sacroiliac joint. It is more common than the left OP position.
  • Direct OP position - When the occiput points directly towards the sacrum.

All three positions may be primary (present before the onset of labor) or secondary (develops after the onset of labor). 

Other options:

Option A: Brow presentation is a rare type of cephalic presentation where the position of the head is in between full flexion and full extension. The part of the head between the orbital ridge and the anterior fontanel presents at the pelvic inlet.

Option B: Knee presentation is a type of breech presentation. Here, the thighs are extended but the knees are flexed, presenting at the pelvic inlet. The head will be palpable as a hard globular mass at the fundus.

Option D: Right dorso-anterior position is when the fetal back is directed anteriorly. This occurs in a transverse lie. On examination, the abdomen appears wide, and a hard plane of resistance is felt. The fundus extends just above the umbilicus. The head is felt in one iliac fossa and the breech is felt in the other.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A primi at term presented with labor pain and multiple painful vesicular lesions on her vulva. No rashes were found on other parts of the body. What will be the management of this case?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a primi in labor pain with multiple, painful vesicular lesions on her vulva is suggestive of an active herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. Management involves the administration of acyclovir and elective cesarean section.

HSV infection in pregnancy can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2 and transmitted by sexual contact. The infection can be primary, nonprimary, first episode, and recurrent.  

HSV infection (both HSV 1 and 2) during pregnancy has a risk of vertical transmission of the infection to the fetus. The risk is higher in the primary than in the recurrent infection. The maximum risk of fetal infection is during labor, although it can occur in utero and post-natally from direct contact. 

Suspicious lesions should be sent for PCR testing or culture. Antiviral treatment with acyclovir should be given if found positive. Women with no active genital lesions, asymptomatic, or those with active lesions in non-genital areas can undergo normal labor and delivery. 

Management of HSV infection during pregnancy:

  • Oral acyclovir or valacyclovir for primary or recurrent infections during pregnancy.
  • IV acyclovir followed by oral acyclovir for severe or disseminated infection
  • Oral analgesics or topical anesthetics for pain relief
  • Catheterization for urinary retention

Cesarean delivery reduces the risk of vertical transmission during labor and is indicated in:

  • Cases of active genital lesions - both primary and recurrent
  • Prodromal symptoms like vulval itching or burning

Other options:

Option B: The presene of active lesions is a contraindication for induction of labor.

Option C: Spontaneous delivery is contraindicated in the presence of active lesions.

Option D: Even after treatment with acyclovir, normal delivery is not indicated owing to the risk of dormant viral transmission to the fetus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A 30-year-old married woman came for an infertility evaluation. On performing further investigations, intramural fibroids of sizes 7x5cm and 5x3cm were seen at the right and left cornual ends of the uterus. Her husband's semen analysis was found to be normal. What is the appropriate management of this case?
questions.explanation:
The most appropriate management for a woman with infertility due to intramural fibroids at both the cornual ends of the uterus is myomectomy. The infertility, in this case, is due to the fibroids blocking the right and left cornua of the uterus.

Myomectomy refers to the removal of fibroids and preserving the uterus. It is indicated in women presenting with infertility, those who desire pregnancy, or those who wish to retain the uterus.

Intracavitary fibroids can be resected via the hysteroscopic approach, while subserosal or intramural fibroids require laparotomy or laparoscopic myomectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Uterine artery embolization is not done in this case, as it may decrease fertility, as a result of pelvic adhesions. It is a technique in which polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), gel foam particles, or metal coils are injected into the uterine arteries. This embolization reduces vascularity and the size of the fibroid. It is best suited to control menorrhagia in multiparous women.

Option C: Artificial reproductive techniques are not indicated in this case as infertility is seen to be due to the fibroids blocking the cornual ends of the uterus. However, it may be considered at a later stage.

Option D: GnRH analogs when used for 6 months, can reduce the tumor size by targeting the growth effects of estrogen and progesterone. It can be used in women with infertility caused by cornual fibroids. They are often used preoperatively to reduce the size of the fibroid and facilitate a hysteroscopic approach to surgery. However, it is expensive and can cause menopausal symptoms if used for >6 months. Fibroids are known to regrow 3-4 months after stopping the therapy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A 28-year-old married woman who is anxious to conceive presents with copious vaginal discharge, without any itching. Her last menstrual period was 13 days ago. What is the cause of her vaginal discharge?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a young woman with copious, non-pruritic (without itching) vaginal discharge occurring 13 days after menstrual period (period of ovulation) is most likely to be leucorrhoea (physiological).

The term leucorrhoea can be used in conditions where normal vaginal secretion is increased in amount. An increase in this normal vaginal secretion develops physiologically:

  • At puberty
  • At ovulation
  • During pregnancy
  • During the premenstrual phase, occasionally

It may be cervical or vaginal in origin. A speculum examination of the vagina can distinguish between the two. If the discharge is cervical in origin, an excessive mucoid discharge will be visible at the external os.

Normal discharge appears clear or white, without any odor or itching, and will have a pH of 3.8-4.2.

Other options:

Option A: Candidiasis is caused by infection with Candida albicans and presents with pruritus, burning, and dysuria with vulvar erythema, edema, and excoriations. A curdy white discharge will be present. 

Option B: Bacterial vaginosis is caused by an alteration in the normal vaginal flora and presents without itching and a malodorous grey-white discharge. It is diagnosed using Amsel's criteria, where at least three of the four following criteria should be present to confirm the diagnosis:

  • Homogenous vaginal discharge
  • Vaginal pH > 4.5
  • Amine-like odor on adding KOH (Whiff test positive)
  • Clue cells (>20% of cells)

Option C: Trichomoniasis is caused by Trichomonas vaginalis and presents with a copious, frothy, offensive yellow-green discharge with vaginal soreness or irritation and urinary frequency. On examination, the vagina looks red and inflamed. The inflamed cervix looks like a strawberry with punctate hemorrhagic spots.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A patient developed atonic postpartum hemorrhage after a normal vaginal delivery. She was shifted to the OT and the obstetrician planned ligation of vessels to arrest the bleeding. What is the order of ligation of the blood vessels supplying the uterus?
options: Uterine artery - Ovarian artery - Internal iliac artery
Uterine artery - Ovarian artery- External iliac artery
Uterine artery - Ovarian artery - Vaginal artery
Uterine artery - pudendal artery - Vaginal artery
questions.correct_answer: Uterine artery - Ovarian artery - Internal iliac artery
questions.explanation:
The order of ligation of vessels to arrest bleeding in atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is the uterine artery - ovarian artery - internal iliac artery.

The ascending branch of the uterine artery is ligated between the upper and lower segments of the uterus, at the lateral border. If the bleeding continues, the ovarian and uterine artery anastomosis is ligated just below the ovarian ligament. If the bleeding still persists, the anterior division of the internal iliac artery is ligated 5 cm distal to the common iliac bifurcation.  

Unilateral or bilateral ligation of the internal iliac artery ligation causes a reduction in the pulse pres­sure in the arteries distal to the ligation. This increases the chances of hemostasis via pressure and clot formation.

Surgical methods to control PPH are outlined as stepwise uterine devascularization procedures:

  • Compression sutures: B-Lynch suture
  • Ligation of uterine arteries
  • Ligation of ovarian and uterine anastomosis
  • Ligation of internal iliac artery
  • Angiographic embolization of the bleeding vessel

Pelvic packing (usually done prior to embolization) and hysterectomy are other surgical methods employed to control PPH.

questions.question: A teenage patient presented with a history of dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. On ultrasonography, a transverse vaginal septum was seen. What is the most common complication that can be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The most common complication that can be seen in this patient is endometriosis.

Transverse vaginal septum leads to obstructed flow of menstrual blood. This may lead to retrograde menstruation, which increases the likelihood of the development of endometriosis, according to Sampson's theory of endometriosis.

Transverse vaginal septum occurs as a result of the failure of Müllerian duct fusion or failure of vaginal plate canalization. It may be obstructive or non-obstructive. The commonest site of a transverse septum is the junction between the upper and middle third of the vagina.

Patients with an obstructive or imperforate vaginal septum present with symptoms similar to the imperforate hymen. Symptoms include amenorrhoea, cyclical abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, and a palpable pelvic mass. The vagina may appear shortened and the cervix may not be identifiable. Secondary sexual characteristics appear normal. The diagnosis can be confirmed with ultrasound or MRI.

There is an increased risk of endometriosis. Other complications such as pyomucocolpos, pyometra, and pyosalpinges can also develop in infants with obstructive vaginal septums. 

Treatment is by manual dilatation of the perforation or surgical excision of the septum. 

Other options:

Option B: Tubo-ovarian abscess develops in pelvic inflammatory disease.

Option C: Dermoid cysts are cystic ovarian tumors that are often associated with mucinous cystadenomas.

Option D: Theca lutein cysts are found in association with hydatidiform moles, choriocarcinoma, and gonadotropin or clomiphene citrate therapy. They regress with the management of the mole and choriocarcinoma and discontinuation of gonadotropin therapy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: A 28-year old pregnant woman came for a routine antenatal check-up in her second trimester. Four years back, she delivered 2 healthy full-term twins. What would her obstetric score be?
questions.explanation:
The obstetric score of a pregnant woman who previously delivered twins would be G2P1 (gravida 2 para 1).

The term gravida refers to the number of times the woman has been pregnant, irrespective of whether it crossed the period of viability. The current pregnancy is included in this count. Since she has been pregnant once before with twins and is currently pregnant now, gravida will be 2.

The term para refers to the number of previous pregnancies reaching a period of viability (gestation of 28 weeks). It does not increase to a higher number if multiples (twins/triplets) are delivered in a given pregnancy and still count as one birth. A current pregnancy, if any, is not included in this count. Therefore, para here will be 1 since she had one birth of twins and the present pregnancy is not counted.

Both gravidity and parity refer to the pregnancies and not the fetuses.

Note: The period of viability is when the fetus is capable of independent existence. The WHO defines it to be 24 weeks while the Indian definition is 28 weeks.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman who is on oral contraceptive pills for contraception has forgotten to take her pills on 4 different days in the last 2 weeks. She presents to the primary health center, asking for advice. What would you suggest to her?
options: Take 4 pills now, continue the schedule, use barrier method of contraception
Take 1 pill now, continue the schedule, and use barrier method of contraception
Take 1 pill now, use barrier method, and consider emergency contraception in case of recent intercourse
Discard the pack, start a new pack with alternate method of contraception
questions.correct_answer: Discard the pack, start a new pack with alternate method of contraception
questions.explanation:
A woman who has missed 4 oral contraceptive pills in the last two weeks should take one hormonal pill as soon as possible and finish all hormonal pills in the pack as scheduled, throw away the 7 non-hormonal pills in a 28-pill pack and start a new pack the next day. 

Missed pills Management

Missed 1 or 2 pills/ started new pack 1 or 2 days late?

 

You have two options: take one hormonal pill right away, or take two pills at your usual scheduled time. 

The risk of pregnancy is minimal to none.

 

Missed 3 or more pills in the first or second week/started new pack 3 or more days late?

Take one hormonal pill immediately and then continue taking your pills as scheduled. 

Make sure to use a backup method of contraception for the next seven days.

Additionally, if you've had sexual intercourse within the last 72 hours, consider taking emergency contraceptive pills.

 
Missed 3 or more pills in the third week?

Take one hormonal pill as soon as you can and complete the entire pack of hormonal pills according to the schedule. 

Discard the seven non-hormonal pills in a 28-pill pack. 

Begin a new pack the following day.

 
Missed any nonhormonal pills? (last 7 pills in 28-pill pack)

Dispose of any missed non-hormonal pills. 

Continue taking your combination oral contraceptives (COCs), one pill each day. 

Begin the new pack as you normally would.

 

If any non-hormonal pills were missed, she can discard the remaining pills. Start the new pack of oral contraceptives and continue taking as usual.

If she vomits within 2 hours of taking a pill, another pill from the pack should be taken as soon as possible. After that, continue taking the pills as scheduled. If the vomiting or diarrhea persists for >2 days, follow the instructions for 1 or 2 missed pills as mentioned above.

The contraceptive method should be discontinued and changed in the following situations:

  • Unexplained or prolonged heavy vaginal bleeding that suggests an underlying condition not related to the method
  • Starting anticonvulsant medication or treatment with rifampicin
  • Migraines
  • Non-ambulatory conditions lasting for >1 week like major surgery, leg in a cast, etc. Combined oral contraceptives can be restarted 2 weeks after ambulation.
  • Suspected heart or liver disease, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis, stroke, breast cancer, diabetes, or gall bladder disease

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female patient, on treatment for infertility, came with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and mild vaginal bleeding. Her beta hCG level was 2800 mIU/mL. On ultrasound, a 3cm mass was seen in the left adnexa. It contained a gestational sac with no fetal cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
questions.explanation:
A patient on infertility treatment, with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding with beta hCG levels of 2800 mIU/mL, and a gestational sac in the left adnexa points to the diagnosis of unruptured ectopic pregnancy and the most appropriate management is single-dose methotrexate.

A pregnancy is considered ectopic if implantation occurs at a site outside the uterine cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.

Management of ectopic pregnancy: 

Expectant management: Ectopic pregnancies measuring <3 cm and with declining beta hCG levels initially <1500 mIU/mL may resolve without inter­vention and can be managed expectantly. 

Medical management with single or multiple-dose methotrexate is preferred if:

  • Hemodynamic stability
  • Serum beta-hCG ≥1500 mIU/ml and ≤5000 mIU/mL
  • Mean sac diameter <3.5cm with no fetal cardiac activity detected on transvaginal ultrasound.
  • Patients are willing and able to comply with post-treatment follow-up and have access to emergency medical services within a reasonable time frame in case of a deterioration in the clinical status.

Methotrexate(MTX) can be given as a single IM dose of 50 mg/m2 or as a multiple-dose regimen of 1mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, and 7.

Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

  • Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met
  • Gestational sac >3.5 cm
  • Fetal cardiac activity present
  • Beta hCG > 5000 mIU/mL
  • Significant pain and hemoperitoneum 
  • Failure of expectant or medical management
  • Clinical status of patient warrants urgent intervention
  • Doubtful compliance with medical management 

Milking of the tube through the fimbriae carries a high risk of bleeding, damage to the tube, the persistence of trophoblastic tissue, and recurrence of ectopic pregnancy.

A 30-year-old woman on oral contraceptives for the past 6 months presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhea. What would be the best method of assessing the gestational age of this patient?

LMP- Last menstrual period

USG- Ultrasonography
questions.explanation:
The best method of assessing the gestational age of a patient on oral contraceptives with 6 weeks of amenorrhea is by measuring the crown-rump length (CRL) using ultrasonography.

Gestational age refers to the duration of pregnancy calculated from the first day of the LMP. It is usually expressed in weeks. Following the use of oral contraceptives, ovulation may have been later than 2 weeks after the LMP. Therefore, gestational age calculated with the help of LMP will be inaccurate.

First-trimester ultrasound measurement of CRL is the best method to assess gestational age. It is measured from the vertex to the coccyx.

  • CRL (in mm) + 6.5 = gestational age in weeks (or)
  • CRL (in mm) + 42 days = gestational age in days.

Trimester

Parameter

1st

2nd and 3rd 
  • Biparietal diameter (BPD)
  • Abdominal Circumference (AC)
  • Head Circumference (HC)
  • Femur Length. (FL) 
Other options:
 
Option B: Adding 280 days to the LMP will provide the expected delivery date (EDD). Adding 9 months + 7 days to the LMP or 280 days to the LMP is Naegele’s formula for calculating the EDD.
 
Option C: Measurement of fundal height in cm (with a variation of 1-2cm) is roughly equal to the gestational age in weeks, after 24 weeks of pregnancy. This is measured from the superior border of the symphysis pubis to the top of the uterine fundus when the bladder is empty.

questions.question: 1. Identify the manoeuvre shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
The maneuver shown in the image is Lovset's maneuver, used for the delivery of extended arms in breech presentation. The principle of this maneuver is based on the curved birth canal. The shoulder placement favorable for this maneuver is: * anterior shoulder - above the symphysis pubis * posterior shoulder - below the sacral promontory. Rotating the trunk while keeping the back anterior and applying downward traction brings the posterior shoulder under the symphysis pubis. The technique followed in Lovset's maneuver is  * The baby is grasped with both hands using a femoropelvic grip, keeping the thumbs parallel to the vertebral column. The maneuver should start only when the inferior angle of the anterior scapula is visible underneath the pubic arch. * The baby is lifted slightly to cause lateral flexion. The trunk is rotated 180°, keeping the back anterior and maintaining downward traction. * The trunk is then rotated in the reverse direction, keeping the back anterior, to deliver the former anterior shoulder under the symphysis pubis. Lovset's maneuver can be employed in all types of arm displacement. It does not involve any intrauterine manipulation. These factors make it a preferred maneuver. Pearl PM1839: Maneuvers for breech delivery Pinard’s manoeuvre  It is used for the delivery of extended legs in case of breech delivery. Technique: * Flex and abduct the popliteal fossa * Catch hold of the ankle * Pull down along with abduction

  Lovset’s manoeuvre It is used for the delivery of extended arms in case of a breech presentation. Technique: * Hold the sacrum with the thumb, and the hips and pelvis with other fingers. * Turn the infant 90 degrees to bring the shoulder under pubic symphysis and deliver the anterior shoulder. * Then counter-rotate 180 degrees to engage and deliver the posterior shoulder. 

  Modified Prague’s manoeuvre It is used in breech presentations to deliver the aftercoming head when the back of the fetus fails to rotate to the symphysis. Technique: * Grasp the shoulders of the baby from below with two fingers of one hand. * Draw the feet up and over the maternal abdomen with the other hand.

  Burns-Marshall method It is used for delivery of aftercoming head in case of breech presentation. Technique: * Allow the baby to hang by its own weight. * When the nape of the neck is visible under the pubic arch, grasp the baby by the ankles with a finger in between the two. * Swing the baby in an arc in an upward and forward direction.

  Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit technique It is another method that can be used in the delivery of aftercoming head in case of breech presentation. It is also called malar flexion and shoulder traction. Technique: * Place the baby on the supinated left arm with limbs hanging on either side. * Place the index and middle fingers of the left hand on either side over the malar bones. * Place the ring and the little finger of the pronated right hand on the child’s right shoulder, index finger on the left shoulder and middle finger over the suboccipital region. * Traction is given in the downward and backward direction till the nape of the neck is visible. * Thereafter, the baby is carried in an upward and forward direction towards the mother’s abdomen.

  Mnemonic: * Extend the arm to express Love(Lovset's) * Put the fingers in popliteal fossa for Pinard's(P for P)

questions.question: 2. The hysterectomy specimen of a 65 year old patient is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in this 65-year-old woman’s hysterectomy specimen is endometrial carcinoma. In elderly, postmenopausal women, an irregular, friable growth filling the endometrial cavity with myometrial invasion strongly suggests endometrial carcinoma. Endometrial cancer may be localised or diffuse. It may appear as a nodule, polyp or diffuse lesion involving the entire uterine cavity. The risk factors include PCOS, HRT, obesity, hypertension and diabetes.  About 7-10% cases are asymptomatic. Other clinical features include: * Postmenopausal bleeding/discharge (most common) * Menorrhagia or irregular periods in perimenopausal women * Late features include pain and an abdominal lump * On per vaginal exam, the uterus may be normal or bulky (due to tumour, fibroid, or pyometra) * An adnexal mass may be present, usually feminizing ovarian tumour or metastasis * Advanced disease presents as bulky cervix, patulous os, growth protruding through os * Vaginal or suburethral metastatic nodules can rarely be present Other options:  Option A: Adenomyosis is characterized by the presence of endometrium in the walls of the uterus. The uterus appears symmetrically enlarged to not more than 14 weeks size. The cut section may show only a localized nodular enlargement. Most of the time, the affected area reveals a peculiar, diffuse, striated and noncapsulated involvement of the myometrium with tiny dark haemorrhagic areas in between.  The hysterectomy specimen of adenomyosis is shown below:

questions.question: 3. A 55-year post-menopausal woman presents to the OPD for a routine BP checkup. Her BP was 170/100 mm Hg. She also complains of bloodstained discharge per vagina. What is the next best step of management?
options: Reassure her that some discharge is normal at this age
Immediate pelvic examination, TVS and pap smear
Immediate referral to a cardiologist to control BP
questions.correct_answer: Immediate pelvic examination, TVS and pap smear
questions.explanation:
The next best step of management is immediate pelvic examination, TVS and pap smear.  A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presenting with blood-stained vaginal discharge should be thoroughly evaluated to rule out endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy of the genital tract. Additionally, her hypertension (BP 170/100 mm Hg) is a recognised risk factor for endometrial carcinoma. Other risk factors include obesity, diabetes, polycystic ovarian syndrome, older age, early age of menarche, late age of menopause, nulliparity, and long-term contraceptive use.  As part of the evaluation, a pelvic examination is performed, which may reveal any abnormality in the lower genital tract such as an enlarged uterus, abnormal cervix or adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is performed to assess endometrial thickness and detect any endometrial pathology like an endometrial polyp. An endometrial thickness of more than 4 mm indicates the need of endometrial biopsy. A Pap smear is done to screen for cervical abnormalities and exclude cervical cancer.

Other options: Option A: Reassurance is not appropriate because postmenopausal bleeding is never normal. Option C: Referral to a cardiologist is also not the immediate step, as her blood pressure, though high, is not an acute emergency in this setting. Option D: Proceeding directly to hysterectomy without confirming the diagnosis is incorrect. The appropriate next step is to establish the cause of post-menopausal bleeding and exclude malignancy.

questions.question: 4. A 32-year-old with gestational diabetes mellitus and fetal macrosomia is in labour, the head is delivered, but the shoulders are stuck even after 1 minute. What is the sequence of manoeuvres?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario with a delay in delivery of the baby's shoulders for more than 1 minute after delivery of the head indicates shoulder dystocia, and the correct sequence for managing shoulder dystocia is: McRobert’s manoeuvre → Rubin manoeuvre → Gaskin manoeuvre → Zavanelli manoeuvre. Shoulder dystocia occurs when either the anterior or the posterior fetal shoulder gets impacted on the maternal pelvis or on the sacral promontory. The diagnosis is made on the basis of: * Definite recoil of the head back against the perineum (turtle neck sign) * Failure of spontaneous restitution of fetal head * Fetal face becomes plethoric * Failure of shoulder to descend Management of labour in case of shoulder dystocia: * McRoberts Maneuver: Abduct and sharply flex the maternal thighs onto the abdomen, which straightens the lumbosacral angle, rotates the pelvis, frees the impacted shoulder, and increases the available space (image below). Along with this maneuver, suprapubic pressure is applied, which directs the fetal head posteriorly to reduce the shoulder diameter and rotate it into the oblique plane.

* Rubin’s Maneuver: Rotate the easily accessible fetal shoulder, usually the posterior shoulder, to help release the impacted shoulder (image below).

* Woods Corkscrew Maneuver: Rotate the posterior shoulder 180° in a corkscrew fashion to align it for delivery (image below).

* Extraction of the posterior arm is done with the help of Jacquemier maneuver. * Gaskin Maneuver: Place the mother on her hands and knees (all fours position) to increase pelvic dimensions and allow downward traction on the posterior shoulder to free it. * If other measures fail, the fetus can be pushed back into the uterus for cesarean delivery (Zavanelli manoeuvre), the clavicle can be fractured to reduce shoulder girth (cleidotomy), or, rarely, symphysiotomy may be performed. questions.question: 5. A primigravida at 37 weeks presents with decreased foetal movements for 1 day. NST showed one acceleration in 20 minutes and no decelerations. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
The next step is to continue NST for 40 minutes.  At 37 weeks, a non-stress test (NST) with only one acceleration in 20 minutes is considered non-reactive. However, before confirming any abnormality, the NST should be extended to 40 minutes.  In non-stress test (NST), a continuous electronic monitoring of the fetal heart rate along with recording of fetal movements (cardiotocography) is undertaken. There is an observed association of FHR acceleration with fetal movements, which when present, indicates a healthy fetus.  When two or more accelerations of more than 15 beats per minute above the baseline and longer than 15 seconds in duration are present in a 20-minute observation, it is intrepreted as reactive. On the other hand, a nonreactive NST is not always ominous and can be seen with a sleeping fetus. Hence, before concluding that a test is nonreactive, a 40 minute or longer tracing should be performed. Other options: Option A: Induction of labour is not indicated at this stage because the NST has not yet been confirmed abnormal. Reactivity may still occur with extended monitoring. Option C: Emergency LSCS is indicated only if there is clear evidence of acute fetal distress, which is not present here.  Option D: Instrumental delivery applies when the woman is in the second stage of labour. This patient is not in labour, so it’s not appropriate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology (OBGY)
questions.question: 6. A 25 year-old female has regular 28-day cycles. Which of these hormonal patterns will be seen during day 21-25 of her cycle?
options: Increased estrogen, decreased progesterone, low LH, high FSH
Decreased estrogen and increased progesterone, high FSH and low LH
Increased estrogen and progesterone, low FSH and LH
Decreased estrogen and increased progesterone, low FSH and LH
questions.correct_answer: Increased estrogen and progesterone, low FSH and LH
questions.explanation:
During days 21-25 of her menstrual cycle that is, during the luteal phase, there will be increased estrogen and progesterone and low FSH and LH. The menstrual cycle is characterized by distinct hormonal changes across its different phases: * In the proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle, the endometrium is under the control of oestrogen. The Graafian follicle secretes 17-β-oestradiol, which produces proliferative changes in the endometrium. This oestrogen produces proliferative changes in the endometrium, secretes inhibin which inhibits further secretion of FSH, and stimulates LH receptors in the theca cells while also stimulating the anterior pituitary to secrete LH. * At ovulation (which occurs around day 14), the maximum peak of oestrogen secretion is seen about 48 hours before ovulation, whereas the LH surge occurs about 24–36 hours before ovulation. LH causes rupture of the follicle and formation of the corpus luteum. * In the luteal phase (in this case), the ruptured follicle forms the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone. As a result, progesterone levels rise markedly, while oestrogen is also moderately increased. These high levels exert negative feedback, so FSH and LH remain low. * In the menstrual phase, in the absence of pregnancy, the corpus luteum regresses, leading to a decline in both oestrogen and progesterone levels. This fall removes the negative feedback, and gonadotropins begins to rise again, initiating recruitment of new follicles for the next cycle.

questions.question: 7. A 65-year-old woman presented with abdominal swelling and discomfort. Ultrasonography showed ascites and a multiloculated, predominantly cystic swelling with papillary projections. CA-125 was 1035IU/mL. The gross image of the resected mass is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is serous cystadenocarcinoma, a common epithelial ovarian cancer seen in postmenopausal women. This patient’s presentation with abdominal swelling, ascites, ultrasonography showing a multiloculated cystic mass with papillary projections and the gross image showing a large, multilocular cystic mass is most suggestive of serous cystadenocarcinoma. The markedly elevated CA-125 level (1035 IU/mL) further supports the diagnosis, as this tumour marker is typically raised in epithelial ovarian cancers like the serous type.  Other options:  Option A: Granulosa cell tumor are sex cord-stromal tumors that are hormonally active and often produce estrogen, leading to symptoms such as abnormal uterine bleeding or endometrial hyperplasia, which are not seen in this patient. Additionally, granulosa cell tumors rarely cause massive ascites, and they typically secrete inhibin, which is a marker for this tumour. Option B: Sertoli–Leydig cell tumour are rare ovarian tumours that are androgen-producing, which causes defeminization followed by masculinization. They usually present with features such as flattening of breasts, amenorrhea, hirsutism, enlargement of the clitoris, and even breaking of the voice. Imaging often shows a gross appearance like that of other mesenchymomas, and CA-125 is usually not markedly elevated. Option C: Immature teratoma is a rare tumour containing elements from multiple germ layers. They are mostly solid tumours with a trabeculated appearance. The solid part of the tumour contains cartilage, bone, and muscle, whereas hair and sebaceous material are found in the cystic spaces. A rudimentary eye can also be seen. They are generally malignant, whereas mature teratomas like dermoid cysts are benign. They are not commonly associated with papillary projections, massive ascites, or markedly raised CA-125, which are hallmarks of epithelial ovarian cancers like serous cystadenocarcinoma. questions.question: 8. A primigravida suffers atonic postpartum haemorrhage during labour. After initial measures and medical management failed, what is the next best step of management that can be done in the labour room?
questions.explanation:
In a primigravida with atonic PPH where initial measures like uterine massage and medical management have failed, the next best step of management that can be done in the labour room is balloon tamponade. For balloon tamponade, Foley catheter, Bakri balloon, Condom catheter or Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is inserted into the uterine cavity and the balloon is inflated with normal saline (200-500 mL). It reduces PPH by stimulating uterine contraction and exerting direct hemostatic pressure (tamponade effect) to the open uterine sinuses. It is kept for 4-6 hours. This can avoid hysterectomy in most cases. The given image shows Bakri balloon tamponade:



The following are the steps used in controlling postpartum haemorrhage: * Feel the uterus to know the cause of the haemorrhage. If the uterus feels flabby, bleeding is likely to be due to atonicity. If it is firm and contracted, it is likely to be traumatic in origin. * In case of an atonic uterus, massage the uterus and start the patient on oxytocin drips or methergine.  * If the uterus remains atonic, manual exploration of the uterus is done for removing any retained placental fragments. Blood transfusion is started and oxytocin drips are continued. Other uterotonic agents can also be given. * Uterine massage and bimanual compression * Uterine tamponade using a hydrostatic balloon catheter (balloon tamponade) * Surgical methods to control PPH are outlined as stepwise uterine devascularization procedures: * Compression sutures: B-Lynch suture * Ligation of uterine arteries * Ligation of ovarian and uterine anastomosis * Ligation of internal iliac artery * Angiographic embolization of the bleeding vessel *   Hysterectomy

questions.question: 9. A G2P1L1 suffers cord prolapse during labour. Cervix was 5cm dilated and cord pulsations were present. What is the next best step in management?
options: Elevate buttocks, tilt head back and fill bladder
Push the cord back into the vagina and pack
questions.correct_answer: Elevate buttocks, tilt head back and fill bladder
questions.explanation:
The best step in management of cord prolapse with pulsations present is to relieve pressure on the cord immediately. This is done by elevating the buttocks and tilting head back (trendelenberg position), and filling the bladder with fluid. These measures lift the presenting part off the cord and improve blood flow. Vago's method is used in cord prolapse to alleviate pressure on the cord. Vagos method is also known as the bladder-filling method. Here, the bladder is distended with saline to push the presenting part higher up, thereby preventing compression in case of cord prolapse. The bladder is filled with 400–750 mL of normal saline with a Foley’s catheter. Then, the balloon is inflated and the catheter is clamped. The management algorithm for cord prolapse is based on three important factors: * Living or dead baby * Viability of the baby * Degree of cervical dilatation The definitive treatment for cord prolapse is delivery by cesarean section when the baby is alive and mature as in this clinical scenario. Reconfirming if the baby is alive before the incision is important to prevent unnecessary trauma of surgery. * If immediate safe vaginal delivery is possible -  * When the fetal head is engaged - delivery by forceps. Ventouse is not ideal in such circumstances, as it takes a longer time  * Breech presentation - the delivery is to be completed by breech extraction * Transverse lie - the internal podalic version, followed by breech extraction * When immediate safe vaginal delivery is not possible: * Oxytocin infusion is stopped * IV fluids, oxygen by face mask, and continuous fetal monitoring * Relieve pressure on the cord by: * Manual elevation of the fetal presenting part using two fingers or the whole hand through the vagina. * Positioning of the patient in a steep Trendelenburg position, exaggerated Sim’s position, or knee-chest position. * Vagos method: Foley catheter is placed and the bladder is filled with 500-750 mL of saline, and then clamped. The patient’s enlarging bladder provides upward pressure on the fetus and alleviates the compression of the cord. * Funic reduction: Gentle manual repositioning of the cord into the uterus. It is not preferred nowadays. * Tocolysis can be considered if there is a prolonged interval before delivery * If the baby is dead - * * Reconfirmation with ultrasound * Spontaneous delivery when death is confirmed * Destructive operations are rarely needed The management algorithm for cord prolapse is given below:

Other options: Option B: Wait and watch is not an option because ongoing compression can quickly lead to fetal hypoxia and death. Option C: Oxytocin to accelerate delivery is not useful at 5 cm dilation because vaginal delivery will not happen immediately. The baby will not be delivered fast enough to prevent damage. Option D: Pushing the cord back and packing is avoided as it may increase trauma and worsen compression, leading to more harm.

questions.question: 10. What is the order of closure in a mediolateral episiotomy?
questions.explanation:
The correct order of closure in a mediolateral episiotomy is Mucosa → Muscle → Skin. The repair of a mediolateral episiotomy is done in three layers. The repair is to be done in the following order * Vaginal mucosa and submucosal tissues * Perineal muscles * Skin and subcutaneous tissues The vaginal mucosa is sutured first. The apex of the episiotomy is identified, and an anchor stitch is placed. Thereafter, the vaginal walls are apposed by interrupted sutures with polyglycolic acid suture or chromic catgut, from above downwards till the fourchette is reached. A continuous suture may cause puckering and shortening of the posterior vaginal wall. Care should be taken not to injure the rectum.  The principles to be followed are:  * Perfect hemostasis * To obliterate the dead space * Suture without tension  However, routine episiotomy is not recommended for the management of the 2nd stage of labour. The indications of an episiotomy are: * Rigid inelastic perineum causing arrest or delay in descent of the presenting part as in elderly primigravidae * Anticipating perineal tear due to a big baby, face-to-pubis delivery, breech delivery, shoulder dystocia, and persistent occiput posterior * Operative delivery, like forceps delivery and ventouse delivery * Previous perineal surgery, like pelvic floor repair and perineal reconstructive surgery The image below shows the episiotomy scissors:

Pearl PM0044: Mediolateral Episiotomy It begins within 3 mm of the midline in the posterior fourchette and is directed laterally at an angle of at least 60 degrees from the midline. This yields an incision of 45 degrees off the midline. It is essentially an inflicted second-degree perineal tear. Structures cut in mediolateral episiotomy: * Posterior vaginal wall * Superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles, bulbospongiosus and part of levator ani * Fascia covering those muscles * Transverse perineal branches of pudendal vessels and nerves * Subcutaneous tissue and skin Advantage: Lesser risk of anal sphincter laceration, hence it is preferred over median episiotomy. Disadvantage: Increased blood loss and causes more perineal pain and dyspareunia.

questions.question: 11. A patient presents with 2 months of amenorrhea with enlarged uterus. On examination, there is darkening of areola, prominent Montgomery tubercles, linea nigra is present and there is bluish discolouration of the vagina on PV. How would you categorise these signs in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
This patient’s findings are categorised as probable signs of pregnancy. The patient shows amenorrhea, breast changes (like darkened areola and Montgomery tubercles), linea nigra, and Chadwick’s sign, which are presumptive signs of pregnancy. However, the patient also has uterine enlargement, which is an objective physical change of the uterus and is classified as a probable sign of pregnancy, because it is detectable by the clinician. Although most features are presumptive, the presence of uterine enlargement, which is a probable sign, makes the overall signs of pregnancy beyond purely presumptive, and this patient’s findings can be categorised as probable signs of pregnancy. The signs and symptoms of pregnancy can be categorised into:  * Presumptive signs: These are primarily the features appreciated by the woman and include amenorrhea, frequency of micturition, morning sickness, fatigue, breast changes, skin pigmentation (like linea nigra and chloasma), quickening. * Probable signs: These are mainly detectable physical changes in the uterus observed by the clinician. They include uterine enlargement, changes in shape and consistency of the uterus, Hegar’s sign (softening of the lower uterine segment), Jacquemier’s sign, ballottement, and immunological tests. * Positive (absolute) signs: These are absolute indicators of pregnancy and include palpation of fetal parts, perception of fetal movements by the examiner, auscultation of fetal heart sounds, and ultrasound detection of the gestational sac or embryo. These signs confirm pregnancy beyond doubt. Other options: Option D:  In pseudopregnancy, there is no true pregnancy. It is also called as pseudocyesis, which is a psychological disorder where the woman has the false but firm belief that she is pregnant, although no pregnancy exists. The conspicuous feature is cessation of menstruation. Obstetric examination often excludes pregnancy. Examination with ultrasound and immunological tests for pregnancy is done to exclude pregnancy. questions.question: 12. A 35-year-old P2L2 woman presented with secondary amenorrhoea for 1 year. She had elevated gonadotropic hormones (FSH 36 IU/L, LH 56 IU/L) and decreased AMH (0.05 ng). What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The likely diagnosis is premature ovarian insufficiency, because the patient has secondary amenorrhoea with high FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) and very low AMH, indicating depleted ovarian reserve. Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is defined as loss of oocytes and the surrounding support cells prior to age 40 years. The diagnosis is determined by two serum FSH levels that measure greater than a threshold range of 30 to 40 mIU/mL and are obtained at least 1 month apart. This definition distinguishes POI from the physiologic loss of ovarian function, which occurs with normal menopause. AMH is secreted by the Sertoli cells in the testis and granulosa cells in the ovary. In males, it inhibits the development of the Mullerian system and its absence can result in hermaphroditism. In the female, it helps in follicular development and oocyte maturation. The estimation of serum AMH is used in the study of ovarian reserve in an infertile woman and a woman with secondary amenorrhoea. They strongly correlate with the number of ovarian primordial follicles. This makes AMH the best predictor for measuring ovarian reserve. The AMH values and their interpretation are given below: * Normal value: 2–6.8 ng/mL * Poor ovarian reserve : <1 ng/mL * PCOD and hyperstimulation syndrome: >10 ng/mL The other indicator of ovarian reserve is FSH levels measured in the early follicular phase (between day 2 and day 4 of the menstrual cycle). A value of >10 mIU/mL may indicate significant loss of ovarian reserve. Other options: Option A: PCOS typically shows LH levels raised over 10 IU/mL and normal FSH, hence ruling it out. Option B: Hyperprolactinaemia would cause amenorrhoea, but usually with high prolactin and suppressed gonadotropins, not elevated FSH/LH. Option C: Hyperthyroidism can cause menstrual irregularity, but would not explain high FSH/LH with low AMH.

14 g is the total loading dose of magnesium sulphate given in Pritchard's regimen to manage pre-eclampsia. Magnesium sulphate is used to manage severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. It acts as a membrane stabilizer and neuroprotector. It also reduces motor endplate sensitivity to acetylcholine and blocks neuronal calcium influx. MgSO4 regimens:
Regimen Loading Dose Maintenance Dose
Intramuscular (Pritchard) 4 g (20% solution) IV over 3-5 minute
followed by 10 g (5O%), deep IM
(5 gm in each buttock)		 5 g (5O%) IM 4 hourly in the alternate buttock

Repeat injections are given only if the knee jerks are present, urine output exceeds 30 mL/h and the respiration rate is more than 12/minute. The therapeutic level of serum magnesium is 4-7 mEq/L. questions.question: 14. The resident is performing a manoeuvre in the labour room. Identify the procedure.
questions.explanation:
The procedure shown is controlled cord traction. In the third stage of labour, the placenta is expected to be delivered spontaneously soon following the delivery of the baby. If the placenta is not delivered thereafter, it should be delivered forthwith by controlled cord traction (Brandt-Andrews) technique after clamping the cord while the uterus still remains contracted. In controlled cord traction (modified Brandt-Andrews method), the palmar surface of the fingers of the left hand is placed above the symphysis pubis, approximately at the junction of the upper and lower uterine segment. The body of the uterus is pushed upward and backwards, towards the umbilicus, while with the right hand steady tension is given in downward and backwards direction, holding the clamp until the placenta comes outside the introitus. The procedure is to be adopted only when the uterus is hard and contracted. The third stage of labour includes separation, descent, and expulsion of the placenta with its membranes. According to WHO guidelines, active management of the third stage of labor (AMTSL) has the following components: * Administration of uterotonics within 1 min of delivery. * Controlled cord traction and expulsion of the placenta. * Delayed cord clamping for a minimum of 1-3 minutes to reduce anemia in the fetus. * Intermittent assessment of the uterine tone for early detection of atony.

questions.question: 15. A P1L1 mother with BMI of 35 diagnosed with pre-eclampsia underwent LSCS. What is the ideal agent for prophylaxis of post partum venous thromboembolism?
questions.explanation:
For a P1L1 mother with BMI 35, diagnosed with pre-eclampsia and who underwent LSCS, the risk of postpartum venous thromboembolism (VTE) is high. The ideal agent for prophylaxis in this setting is Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH). Subacutaneous administration of LMWH is used for thromboprophylaxis in immobilized medically ill patients or in those who have undergone major surgery. LMWH is the drug of choice for anticoagulation in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta to cause fetal malformations. It has better bioavailability, longer half-life, predictable dose response and reduced adverse effects like osteoporosis and thrombocytopenia and less frequent dosing. For postpartum anticoagulation, LMWH is given subcutaneously once a day for 6-8 weeks. Oral anticoagulants may be considered postpartum based upon planned duration of therapy, lactation and patient preference.  Other options: Option B: Although effective for long-term anticoagulation, warfarin is not started immediately after delivery due to the risk of initial hypercoagulability, delayed onset of action, and the need for close INR monitoring. Option C and D: Clopidogrel and aspirin are antiplatelet drugs, not anticoagulants. It has limited efficacy in preventing venous thromboembolism compared to LMWH.

questions.question: 16. A 28 year old female who was diagnosed with carcinoma cervix presented with hydroureteronephrosis. What is the stage of the disease?

Carcinoma cervix with hydroureteronephrosis is classified as Stage III B  according to Revised 2018 FIGO staging. Stage III cervical carcinoma may involve the lower 1/3rd of the vagina, with or without pelvic wall extension, may present as hydronephrosis and/or pelvic/paraortic lymph node involvement. It is further staged as follows: * Stage III A: Lower 1/3rd of the vagina involvement, no pelvic wall extension * Stage III B: Pelvic wall involvement with or without hydronephrosis or a non-functioning kidney * Stage III C: Involvement of the pelvic and/or paraaortic lymph nodes * Stage III C1: Metastasis to pelvic lymph node only * Stage III C2: Metastasis to para-aortic lymph nodes Carcinoma cervix can cause ureteral obstruction. Hydronephrosis and uremia can follow and may occasionally be the initial presenting finding. In these cases, ureteral stenting or percutaneous nephrostomy tube insertion is usually required. Kidney function is ideally preserved for chemotherapy. questions.question: 18. A 45-year-old woman presents with delayed cycles and heavy bleeding for the past year. Ultrasonography shows an endometrial thickness of 16 mm. What is the next best step in management?

The next line of management for this patient with an endometrial thickness of 16 mm is an endometrial biopsy.  In perimenopausal women with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), the first priority is to rule out endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, since risk increases with age. In this case, ultrasonography shows an endometrial thickness of 16 mm. For perimenopausal women, an endometrial thickness >10 mm is generally considered abnormal and requires further evaluation. Therefore, the next best step is an endometrial biopsy to establish a tissue diagnosis. In a postmenopausal woman, the normal endometrium should not exceed 4 mm in thickness. If it exceeds 4 mm on ultrasound is considered abnormal and requires histopathological evaluation irrespective of the presence or absence of symptoms to rule out endometrial carcinoma or hyperplasia. Immediate endometrial biopsy is indicated rather than waiting and watching or empirical hormonal therapy. Hysterectomy is not the first-line step without a tissue diagnosis. The methods available to obtain endometrial tissue for histopathological examination are: * Dilation and curettage (D&C) - It is a fractional curettage comprising separate scrapings of endometrium and endocervix not only allows the exact site of malignancy, if present, but also detects the extent of spread of the tumour and staging. It is the best investigation to rule out cancer. The curettage requires general anaesthesia and hospitalization. * Uterine cavity aspiration for endometrial sampling - It is an outpatient procedure that has the additional advantage of avoiding anaesthesia. Pipelle aspirator or Vibra aspirator is used to obtain endometrial sample.  * Hysteroscopy with endometrial aspiration

questions.question: 19. A 30-year-old pregnant female with a history of enlarged inguinal lymph nodes and toxoplasmosis 5 years ago tested positive for IgG to toxoplasmosis. She should ____

The pregnant female should be counselled that there is no risk to the foetus and that pregnancy can be continued. This woman’s IgG positivity for toxoplasmosis reflects a past infection, in her case from 5 years ago, and indicates that she has developed long-term immunity and there is no risk for fetal infection. questions.question: 20. A 35-year-old lady with amenorrhea presents with galactorrhea. She is diagnosed with pituitary adenoma. What is the most probable cause of the condition?

The most probable cause of this condition is decrease in GnRH. In this case, the 35-year-old woman has amenorrhea with galactorrhea, and the underlying cause is a pituitary adenoma, most likely a prolactinoma. The excessive secretion of prolactin in such tumors has a direct inhibitory effect on the hypothalamus. Prolactin inhibits the secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone by the hypothalamus. This inhibition, in turn, suppresses the formation of the pituitary gonadotropic hormones - luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. Prolactinoma usually presents with amenorrhea, infertility, and galactorrhea. If the tumour extends outside the sella, visual field defects or other mass effects may be seen. The diagnosis of prolactinoma is likely with a prolactin level >200 μg/L. An MRI is recommended in all patients who present with hyperprolactinemia. Microadenomas can be managed with regular monitoring of prolactin levels and MRI scans, if fertility is not a requisite. Oral dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine and cabergoline are used for medical management. Resistance or intolerance to these drugs requires surgical debulking. Cases that do not respond to medical or surgical management can be treated with radiotherapy.

In early pregnancy, the crown–rump length is the most accurate method for assessing gestational age. Gestational age refers to the duration of pregnancy calculated from the first day of the LMP. It is usually expressed in weeks. In case of irregular periods, gestational age calculated with the help of LMP will be inaccurate. First-trimester ultrasound measurement of CRL is the best method to assess gestational age. It is measured from the outer margin of the cephalic pole to the rump in the midsagittal plane with the embryo or fetus in a neutral, nonflexed position. The embryofetal crown-rump length in the first trimester is accurate up to ± 5 to 7 days.  CRL measurement is shown in the image below:

On TVS, the gestation sac could be seen as early as 4.5-5 weeks. Fetal gestational age can also be estimated by measuring the Mean Gestational Sac Diameter (MSD ), but it is less accurate than CRL and is only used when the embryo is not yet visible. questions.question: 22. A 30-year-old female came with a history of chronic abdominal discomfort for the past 1 year. The MRI shows the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette of a 30-year-old female with a history of chronic abdominal discomfort for the past 1 year and the MRI showing an enlarged globular uterus with thickening of the junctional zone is suggestive of adenomyosis. Adenomyosis refers to the growth of the endometrium (both stromal and glandular components) directly into the myometrium. It is predominantly seen in multiparous women above the age of 40 years. Patients generally present with menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, pelvic discomfort, and backache, while some patients are asymptomatic. On examination, there is a gross symmetrical enlargement of the uterus corresponding to a 12-14 week size. The uterus is soft and tender on bimanual examination. TVS findings include alternating vertical stripes of hyperechoic and hypoechoic bands, which is called the Venetian blind appearance. On MRI, a diffuse, widened low-intensity junctional zone ≥12 mm predicts adenomyosis with high accuracy, while a junctional zone ≤8 mm excludes it with high accuracy. However, the only definitive mode of diagnosis is histopathological examination. Since most women affected by the condition are past the childbearing age, total hysterectomy is the treatment of choice. Localised excision/Levonorgestrel-containing IUCD can be tried in younger women.

Other options:  Option A: Fibroid clinically presents similarly to adenomyosis, but fibroid is usually focal, well-circumscribed, the uterus can get more enlarged, and the uterine contour is usually irregular. There is no thickening of the junctional zone as seen in the image. Option C: Endometrial polyps are overgrowths of benign endometrial stroma covered by columnar epithelium. They appear as smooth polypoid masses arising from the endometrium into the uterine cavity. The USG below shows a characteristic feeding vessel sign on the colour Doppler.

Option D: Endometriosis is the presence of endometrium at a site outside the endometrial lining. It can be found in ectopic sites such as the ovary, pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, appendix, pelvic lymph nodes, lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) scar endometriosis, umbilicus, and lung. MRI shows haemorrhages, deep pelvic lesions and fibrosis.
